To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a hybrid two-stage PA achieves 16 dB gain, 20 dBm output power, and 52% PAE at 10 GHz; and a monolithic PA achieves 24.7-dB gain, 24.6dBm output power, 52% PA, at 8 GHz.
class-E mode operation of the second stage of two-stage microwave power amplifier can be used to achieve high efficiency at high power levels.
the efficiency optimization of X- band two-stage microwave power amplifier is achieved by using a class-E mode for the output stage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimization of the efficiency of X-band two-staged microwave PAs in which the output stages are designed to operate in the class-E mode.
the design of high efficiency power amplifiers for wireless communications.
the optimization of the power-added efficiency of X-band microwave power amplifiers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the class-AB first-stage PA with the class-E second stage is the optimum choice for high efficiency at X-band frequencies.
, for high-power microwave applications, the use of class-E mode in the output stage of a multistage PA is a promising way to increase efficiency.
the class-E output stage is an excellent choice when high PAE is desired.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the class-E PA is a viable alternative for high-efficiency power amplifier design.
class-E theory is very useful in designing a high-efficiency PA.
the design of high-efficiency microwave PAs is not limited to the class-E topology, and that class-E theory can be used as a design tool for the design of broadband PAs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a class-E second stage can provide a significant improvement in PAE over the class-AB stage, even with the additional loss associated with the class-E output matching network.
the class-E output stage can be used with other stages to improve the efficiency of microwave PAs.
class-E theory can be extended to two-stage PAs, and the resulting design can be implemented using either discrete or monolithic devices.
